fields.claim_quote:
Let $P_f, P_g, P_\RR$ be the [[Definition:URM Program|URM programs]] computing, respectively, the functions $f$ and $g$ and the [[Definition:Characteristic Function of Relation|characteristic function]] $\chi_\RR$.

From [[Recursive Function is URM Computable]], these programs are guaranteed to exist.
fields.explanation:
The complete source permits an arbitrary relation R but asserts existence of a URM program computing its characteristic function. This local assertion is the quoted target. With both branches constant zero, the final function h is recursive; the record does not claim otherwise. Keep the original diagonal relation R(n) iff program n does not halt on input n with output1, and the original total constant-zero branch functions. A supposed characteristic program contradicts its own diagonal case; the explicit zeroing program validates the source premises and supplies a nonvacuous control. The original pairing and four-instruction URM model remain. General pairing and instruction roundtrips, a proved decoder fuel bound, full finite-program roundtrip, and decoder surjectivity connect every finite instruction-list program to its code. Mathlib reflexive transitive closure supplies unbounded finite runs. Deterministic halting uniqueness and the direct all-program nonexistence theorem close the earlier coverage gap.

Thus the claimed program does not exist; the cited theorem applies only when χ_R is recursive.

Separate mathematical remark (not part of the selected formal certificate): the theorem as literally stated, with no hypothesis that R has a recursive (URM-computable) characteristic function, is itself false. With f ≡ 1 and g ≡ 0 the function h defined by the theorem would be the characteristic function χ_R, so a relation R whose characteristic function is not recursive (for example the diagonal relation used above) gives a non-recursive h. The selected certificate instantiates f = g = 0 and refutes only the asserted existence of a program computing χ_R for arbitrary R; with that instantiation h is recursive.
fields.flaw: For the arbitrary relation R in the theorem, a URM program computing its characteristic function is guaranteed to exist.
fields.problem:
Title: Combination of Recursive Functions

Let $f: \N^k \to \N$ and $g: \N^k \to \N$ be [[Definition:Recursive Function|recursive functions]] (not necessarily [[Definition:Total Function|total]]), where $k \ge 1$.

Let $\RR$ be a [[Definition:Relation|$k$-ary relation]] such that:
:if $\map \RR {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k}$ holds, then $\map f {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k}$ is defined
:if $\map \RR {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k}$ does not hold, then $\map g {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k}$ is defined.

Let $h: \N^k \to \N$ be the [[Definition:Function|function]] defined as:
:$\map h {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} = \begin {cases}
\map f {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} & : \text{if } \map \RR {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} \text { holds} \\
\map g {n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_k} & : \text{otherwise}
\end {cases}$
so that $h$ is [[Definition:Total Function|total]].

Then $h$ is [[Definition:Recursive Function|recursive]].

fields.witness: Fix an enumeration of URM programs. Define R(n) iff program n, run on input n, does not halt with output 1. This is a relation on naturals, so it satisfies the sole stated condition that R is arbitrary.

scope_metadata.final_theorem_status: The theorem as literally stated (no hypothesis that R has a recursive characteristic function) is false by a separate elementary argument; the selected certificate refutes only the local existence step, and with f = g = 0 the resulting h is recursive.
scope_metadata.source_kind: ProofWiki proof (Combination of Recursive Functions); load-bearing local step: the programs P_f, P_g, P_R 'are guaranteed to exist' (frozen lines 1, 3) although R is only assumed to be a relation.
scope_metadata.source_scope: The certified target is the unjustified existence of a URM program computing the characteristic function χ_R for arbitrary R, instantiated with the constant-zero branch functions f = g = 0 and the diagonal relation. A separate, uncertified argument (explanation) shows the theorem as literally stated is also false with different branch values; that argument is not the selected formal certificate.
